newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Speculation drove Taiwan's '96 S.Korea gold import.
newsitem.headline: Speculation drove Taiwan's '96 S.Korea gold import.

text.p: Bullion dealers said on Wednesday that much of Taiwan's large 1996 gold imports from South Korea were speculative transshipments by major Korean firms, and that the practice has now been curbed.
Bank of Korea figures showed on Wednesday that Taiwan imported 41.6 tonnes gold from South Korea in 1996, but Taipei bullion dealers said the gold did not originate in South Korea.
"Gold imported from South Korea in 1996 was gold made by other major bullion producers," one dealer said, adding that Switzerland, South Africa and Australia were the main sources.
Imports from South Korea comprised fully 43 percent of Taiwan's total of 95.655 tonnes of gold imports last year.
Many major Korean firms made speculative gold transshipments before the South Korea government began cracking down on the practice in July 1996.

Typically, South Korean bullion houses imported gold on 90- to 120-day deferred payments, then immediately exported the gold at a slight discount and put the money in high-interest money market instruments that more than made up for the discounts.
Significant profits could be made by exploiting the gap between South Korea's interest rates and London's Interbank Offered Rate and re-export tax breaks.
But on July 1, Seoul shortened the deferred payment period to a maximum of 30 days, instantly chilling what had been a booming transshipment business.
Taiwan traders said some scattered trading still existed in South Korea, but on a much smaller scale.

South Korea's gold imports rose 95.2 percent in 1996 to 424.4 tonnes from 217.4 tonnes in 1995, the Bank of Korea said. Its 1996 gold exports surged 116 percent to 427.3 tonnes from 197.8 tonnes in 1995.

Singapore was the biggest buyer of South Korean gold in 1996, taking 143 tonnes. Hong Kong took 113.5 tonnes, Malaysia 60.7 tonnes, Taiwan 41.6 tonnes, Switzerland 27.9 tonnes and Japan 25.3 tonnes, it said.
